meta.title: First 1992 presidential debate (Bush, Clinton, Perot), opening 15:35
meta.speakerNames: Provider labels mapped to names by aligning with the debates.org transcript

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Good evening and welcome to the first of 3 debates among the major candidates for president of the United States sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: The candidates are independent candidate Ross Perot, Governor Bill Clinton, the Democratic nominee, and President George Bush, the Republican nominee.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: I am Jim Lehrer of the MacNeil-Lehrer NewsHour on PBS, and I will be the moderator for this 90-minute event.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: which is taking place before an audience here in the athletic complex on the campus of Washington University in St.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Louis, Missouri. 3 journalists will be asking questions tonight.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: They are John Masic of the Boston Globe, Ann Compton of ABC News, and Sander Van Ocker, a freelance journalist.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: We will follow a format agreed to by representatives of the Clinton and Bush campaigns.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: That agreement contains no restrictions on the content or subject matter of the questions.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Each candidate will have up to 2 minutes for a closing statement.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: The order of those, as well as the questioning, was determined by a drawing.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: The first question goes to Mr.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Perot. He will have 2 minutes to answer, to be followed by rebuttals of 1 minute each from Governor Clinton, and then President Bush.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Gentlemen, good evening.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Good evening, Jim.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: The first topic tonight is what separates each of you from the other.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Mr. Perot, what do you believe tonight is the single most important separating issue of this campaign?

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I think the principal issue that separates me Is that 5.5 million people came together on their own and put me on the ballot.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I was not put on the ballot by either of the two parties.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I was not put on the ballot by any PAC money, by any foreign lobbyist money, by any special interest money.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: This is a movement that came from the people.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: This is the way the framers of the Constitution intended our government to be, a government that comes from the people.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: Over time, we have developed a government that comes at the people.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: Comes from the top down, where the people are more or less treated as objects to be programmed during the campaign with commercials and media events and fear messages and personal attacks and things of that nature.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: The thing that separates my candidacy and makes it unique is that this came from millions of people in 50 states all over this country who wanted a candidate that worked and belonged to nobody but them.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I go into this race as their servant, and I belong to them.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: So this comes from the people.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Governor Clinton, 1-minute response.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: The most important distinction in this campaign is that I represent real hope for change, a departure from trickle-down economics, a departure from tax-and-spend economics, to invest and grow.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: But before I can do that, I must challenge the American people to change.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: And they must decide.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Tonight I say to the president, Mr.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Bush, for 12 years you've had it your way.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: You've had your chance, and it didn't work.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: It's time to change.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I want to bring that change to the American people, but we must all decide first we have the courage to change for hope and a better tomorrow.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Mr.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: President Bush, 1-minute response, sir.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Well, I, I think one thing that distinguishes is experience.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I think we've dramatically changed the world.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I'll talk about that a little bit later.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But the changes are mind-boggling for world peace.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Kids go to bed at night without the same fear of nuclear war.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And change for change's sake isn't enough.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We saw that message in the late '70s, and we heard a lot about change.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And what happened? The misery index went right through the roof.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But I— my economic program, I think, is the kind of change we want.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And the way we're going to get it done is we're going to have a brand-new Congress.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: A lot of them are thrown out because of all the scandals.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I'll sit down with them, Democrats and Republicans alike, and work for my agenda for American renewal, which represents real change.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But I'd say if you had to separate out, I think it's experience at this level.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Governor Clinton, how do you respond on— to the president's On the question— you have 2 minutes on the question of experience.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: He says that is what distinguishes him from the other 2 of you.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I believe experience counts, but it's not everything.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Values, judgment, and the record that I have amassed in my state also should count for something.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I've worked hard to create good jobs and to educate people.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: My state now ranks first in the country in job growth this year.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Fourth in income growth, fourth in the reduction of poverty, third in overall economic performance according to a major news magazine.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: That's because we believe in investing in education and in jobs.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: And we have to change in this country.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: You know, my wife Hillary gave me a book about a year ago in which the author defined insanity as just doing the same old thing over and over again and expecting a different result.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We have got to have the courage to change.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Experience is important, yes.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I've gotten a lot of good experience in dealing with ordinary people over the last year and a month.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I've touched more people's lives and seen more heartbreak and hope, more pain and more promise than anybody else who's run for president this year.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: And I think the American people deserve better than they're getting.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We have gone from 1st to 13th in the world in wages in the last 12 years.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Since Mr. Bush and Mr.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Reagan have been in.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Personal income has dropped while people have worked harder in the last 4 years.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: There have been twice as many bankruptcies as new jobs created.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We need a new approach.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: The same old experience is not relevant.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We're living in a new world after the Cold War, and what works in this new world is not trickle-down, not government for the benefit of the privileged few, not tax and spend, but a commitment to invest in American jobs and American education.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Controlling American health care costs, and bringing the American people together.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: That is what works.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: And you can have the right kind of experience and the wrong kind of experience.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Mine is rooted in the real lives of real people, and it will bring real results if we have the courage to change.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: President Bush, 1 minute to respond.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I just thought of another— another big difference here between me— I don't believe Mr.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Perot feels this way, but I know Governor Clinton did, because I want to accurately quote him.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: He thinks— I think he said that the country is coming apart at the seams.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Now, I know that the only way he can win is to make everybody believe the economy is worse than it is.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But this country is not coming apart at the seams, for heaven's sakes.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We're the United States of America.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We, in spite of the economic problems, we are the most respected economy around the world.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Many would trade for it.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We've been caught up in a global slowdown.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We can do much, much better.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But we ought not to try to convince the American people that America is a country that's coming apart at the seams.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I would hate to be running for president and think that the only way I could win would be to convince every— everybody how horrible things are.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Yes, there are big problems.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And yes, people are hurting.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But I believe that this agenda for American renewal that I have is the answer to do it.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And I believe we can get it done now.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Mr. Romney, Whereas we didn't in the past, because you're going to have a whole brand-new bunch of people in the Congress that are going to have to listen to the same American people I'm listening to.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Mr. Perot, a minute response, sir.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: Well, they've got a point.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I don't have any experience in running up a $4 trillion debt.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I don't have any experience in gridlock government where nobody takes responsibility for anything and everybody blames everybody else.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I don't have any experience in creating the worst public school system in the industrialized world, the most violent, crime-ridden society in the industrialized world, but I do have a lot of experience in getting things done.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: So if we're at a point in history where we want to stop talking about it and do it, I've got a lot of experience in figuring out how to solve problems, making the solutions work, and then moving on to the next one.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I've got a lot of experience in not taking 10 years to solve a 10-minute problem.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: So if it's time for action, I think I have experience that counts.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: If there's more time for gridlock and talk and finger-pointing, I'm the wrong man.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: President Bush, the question goes to you.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: You have 2 minutes.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: And the question is this: Are there important issues of character separating you from these other 2 men?

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I think the American people should be the judge of that.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I think character is a very important question.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I said something the other day where I was accused of being like Joe McCarthy, because I questioned— I put it this way.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I think it's wrong to demonstrate against your own country or organize demonstrations against your own country in foreign soil.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I just think it's wrong.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I— I— Then maybe they say, well, it was a youthful indiscretion.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I was 19 or 20 flying off an aircraft carrier, and that shaped me to be commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And I'm sorry, but demonstrating— it's not a question of patriotism.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: It's a question of character and judgment.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: They get on me.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Bill's gotten on me about read my lips.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And when I make a mistake, I'll admit it.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But he has made— not admitted a mistake.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And I just find it impossible to understand how an American can demonstrate against his own country in a foreign land, organizing demonstrations against it, When young men are held prisoner in Hanoi or kids out of the ghetto were drafted.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Some say, well, you're a little old-fashioned.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Maybe I am, but I just don't think that's right.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Now, whether it's character or judgment, whatever it is, I have a big difference here on this issue.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And so we'll just have to see how it plays out.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: But I, I couldn't do that.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And I don't think most Americans could do that.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: And they all say, well, it was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Well, let's admit it then.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: Say, I made a terrible mistake.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: How could you be Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and have some kid say, when you have to make a tough decision as I did in Panama or in Kuwait, and then have some kid jump up and say, well, I'm not gonna go.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: The Commander-in-Chief was organizing demonstrations halfway around the world during another era.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: So there are differences, but that's about the main area where I think we have a difference.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: I don't know about— I think we have a difference.

segments.speaker: BUSH
segments.text: We'll talk about that a little with Ross here in a bit.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Mr. Perot, you have 1 minute.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I think, uh, American people will make their own decisions on character, and at a time when we have work to do and we need action, I think they need to clearly understand the backgrounds of each person.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: I think the press can play a huge role in making sure that the backgrounds are clearly presented in an objective way.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: then make a decision.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: Certainly anyone in the White House should have the character to be there, but I think it's very important to measure when and where things occurred.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: Did they occur when you were a young person in your formative years, or did they occur while you were a senior official in the federal government?

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: When you're a senior official in the federal government spending billions of dollars of taxpayers' money, and you're a mature individual, and you make a mistake, Then that was on our ticket.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: If you make it as a young man, time passes.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: So I would say, just, you know, look at all 3 of us, decide who you think will do the job, pick that person in November, because believe me, as I've said before, the party's over, and it's time for the cleanup crew.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: And we do have to have change, and people who never take responsibility for anything when it happens on their watch,

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Your time

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: is up.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: Time is up.

segments.speaker: PEROT
segments.text: More later.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: More. Governor Clinton, you have 1 minute.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Ross gave a good answer, but I've got to respond directly to Mr.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Bush. You have questioned my patriotism.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: You even brought some right-wing congressmen into the White House to plot how to attack me for going to Russia in 1969, 1970.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: when over 50,000 other Americans did.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Now, I honor your service in World War II.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I honor Mr. Perot's service in uniform and the service of every man and woman who ever served, including Admiral Crowell, who was your Chairman of the Joint Chiefs and who's supporting me.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: But when Joe McCarthy went around this country attacking people's patriotism, he was wrong.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: He was wrong. And a senator from Connecticut stood up to him named Prescott Bush.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Your father was right to stand up to Joe McCarthy.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: You were wrong to attack my patriotism.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I was opposed to the war, but I love my country.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: And we need a president who will bring this country together, not divide it.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We've had enough division.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I want to lead a unified country.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: All right, we move now to the subject of taxes and spending.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: The question goes to Governor Clinton for a 2-minute answer.

segments.speaker: LEHRER
segments.text: It will be asked by Ann Compton.

segments.speaker: COMPTON
segments.text: Governor Clinton, can you lock in a level here tonight on where middle-income families can be guaranteed a tax cut, or at the very least, at what income level they can be guaranteed no tax increase?

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: The tax increase I have proposed triggers in at family incomes of $200,000 and above.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Those are the people who in the 1980s had their incomes go up while their taxes went down.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Middle-class people, defined as people with incomes of $52,000 and down, had their incomes go down while their taxes went up in the Reagan-Bush years because of 6 increases in the payroll taxes.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: So that is where my income limit would trigger.

segments.speaker: COMPTON
segments.text: So there would be no tax increases below $200,000?

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: My plan, notwithstanding the— my opponent's ad, my plan triggers in at gross incomes, family incomes of $200,000 and above.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Then we want to give modest middle-class tax relief to restore some fairness, especially to middle-class people with families with incomes of under $60,000.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: In addition to that, the money that I raise from upper-income people and from asking foreign corporations just to pay the same income on their income earned in America that American corporations do will be used to give incentives back to upper-income people.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I want to give people permanent incentives, an investment tax credit like President Kennedy and the Congress inaugurated in the early '60s to get industry moving again, a research and development tax credit, a low-income housing tax credit, a long-term capital gains proposal for new business and business expansions.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We've got to have no more trickle-down.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We don't need across-the-board tax cuts for the wealthy for nothing.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We need to say, here's your tax incentive if you create American jobs the old-fashioned way.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: I'd like to create more millionaires than were created under Mr.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: Bush and Mr. Reagan, but I don't want to have 4 years where we have no growth in the private sector, and that's what's happened in the last 4 years.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We're down 35,000 jobs in the private sector.

segments.speaker: CLINTON
segments.text: We need to invest and grow, and that's what I want to do.
